title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is training a generative AI system on copyrighted recordings without obtaining licenses from the rights holders. This happened at the data-collection stage, before any user ever interacted with the product. The failure would have required a legal review of the training corpus before model development began, a step the reporting does not establish was taken.

The deployment produced a publicly available music-generation service capable of producing output resembling specific protected works, including named recordings by The Temptations. Multiple major rights holders brought separate legal actions, and an independent artists' class action survived a motion to dismiss, indicating the scope of alleged infringement extended well beyond a handful of tracks. Sony's allegations cover more than 30,000 recordings, though that figure comes from a lawsuit and is not a court finding.

What is not established is whether Udio's leadership knew the training data was unlicensed, whether any of the lawsuits beyond those settled have been adjudicated on the merits, or what the financial terms of the settlements are. Settlements with Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group resolved those disputes and produced new licensing arrangements, but litigation with Sony and independent artists remained active at the time of reporting.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to resolve disputes over copyrighted music used to train Udio's artificial intelligence system. The case alleged that Udio had used songs like The Temptations' "My Girl" without permission to create similar AI-generated music. Under the new agreement, Udio will launch a platform next year trained exclusively on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs. UMG's leadership stated the settlement reflects their commitment to supporting artists and songwriters while embracing new technologies and business models.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by investors including will.i.am and Mike Krieger, has not disclosed the financial terms of the settlement. The company reported that millions of people have used its platform since launch. This marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label. Artists participating in the new platform will receive compensation, though specific details remain undisclosed. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.
